title: Discharge-Rate and Duration Limits of Batteries for Electric Vertical Take-Off and Landing Aircraft: Failure Boundaries for the Five-Phase Flight Profile
content: Electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft draw their highest currents on discharge, not on charge: in the only public battery dataset cycled under a realistic electric-aircraft duty cycle, the take-off and landing segments are measured at 4.8C and 5.7C on a fresh cell and escalate above 7C as the cells age under a constant-power load. What that dataset does not answer is how long such a rate may be held, and what fails first when it is held too long. This paper answers both. Using an electro-thermal cell model identified from the same dataset, we show that discharge is bounded by four limits with distinct signatures — a power ceiling \(P_{\max}=u^{2}/4R\), terminal voltage, sustained heat rejection, and energy depletion — and that the admissible hold time at a given rate follows in closed form from the lumped thermal transient, \(t_{\max}=\tau_{\mathrm{th}}\ln[\Delta T_{\mathrm{ss}}/(\Delta T_{\mathrm{ss}}-\Delta T_{\mathrm{lim}})]\). Sweeping the five-phase flight profile over rate and duration produces a discharge failure-boundary lookup table \(\Phi_{\mathrm{dis}}\) for four chemistries, quantifying failure severity rather than merely feasibility. Four results matter operationally. The measured duty cycle of the dataset sits essentially on the predicted thermal boundary, so the margin an operator believes they have is small. Duty-cycle structure, not just high-rate energy, sets that boundary: the same 180 s of high-rate discharge is admissible to 7.75 C when split by the cruise interval but only to 6.50 C when contiguous, and the same 0.75–1.5 C of headroom appears in every chemistry, so the cruise segment is thermal-management hardware. The airframe outranks the cell: a vectored-thrust profile leaves 47.6–73.6% of the operating grid flyable depending on chemistry, whereas a hover-dominated profile leaves 1.6–3.5% and cannot fly its 3.8C reference cruise point on any of the four chemistries. And the flight, not the charge, dominates degradation — it accounts for a median 54.8% of per-cycle capacity loss, and the model's per-mission loss reproduces the measured ordering of cycle lives across twelve duty-cycle conditions with \(r=-0.83\).
